headline.title: Pichai bets on always-on agents as autonomy spreads from code to contracts.
headline.summary: Google's CEO says today's AI will look like a flip phone within three years, while OpenAI's Codex Goal Mode and Harvey's contract agents push autonomy from coding into legal work. Beneath the product launches, the day's real weight is scale and disruption: Anthropic's $1.25B-a-month compute bill, a $1B Microsoft-EY push, and California's first-of-its-kind move to shield workers from AI.

stories.title: Pichai says today's AI will look like a flip phone within three years.
stories.toc_summary: In an exclusive I/O 2026 interview, Google's CEO calls the current moment primitive and bets everything on always-on agents.
stories.quick_take: The Rundown sat down with Google CEO Sundar Pichai at I/O 2026 for an exclusive interview on the company's top-to-bottom AI push [1][2]. Pichai argued that within three years today's tools will look as primitive as flip phones, with agents working 24/7 across devices [1]. He pitched Gemini's edge as seamless integration into daily life, and reframed engineering success around orchestrating agents on long-running tasks rather than AI-written code [1].

bullets.label: Creators first:
bullets.text: Pichai said models like Omni let creators express themselves better, but YouTube will stay creator-first and keep its 'human-to-human' connection [1].

bullets.label: Why switch to Gemini:
bullets.text: Asked why an everyday user should move to Gemini, he pointed to seamless integration across daily life, especially agents quietly handling tasks [1].

bullets.label: Agents everywhere:
bullets.text: He predicted agents will run around the clock across devices and be commonplace within three years, making current tech look primitive [1].

bullets.label: Redefining engineering:
bullets.text: For engineers, the success metric won't be AI-written code but agentic coding - directing a team of agents on long-running work [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The throughline is that getting native to these tools is the new literacy - for creators, coders and everyone else [1]. Pichai still insists a human-in-the-loop will matter, but the direction of travel is steep and explicit [1].

stories.title: OpenAI's Codex Goal Mode now runs autonomously for hours or days.
stories.toc_summary: A fresh wave of Codex upgrades pushes the agent from a command-by-command tool toward a goal-driven worker that keeps going on its own.
stories.quick_take: OpenAI dropped another wave of Codex upgrades, headlined by a Goal Mode that lets users set an objective and let the agent work toward it for hours or even days [1][2]. The mode is live across the Codex app, IDE extension and CLI, shifting the system from a tool waiting on each command to an agent that owns a task and delivers a result [1][2]. The release also adds Appshots, locked computer use and advanced annotation [1].

bullets.label: Goal Mode:
bullets.text: Instead of step-by-step instructions, Codex takes a single goal and runs the rest itself, sometimes over multiple days, across app, IDE and CLI [1][2].

bullets.label: Appshots:
bullets.text: Mac users can attach any open app window - its screenshot, text and content - to a Codex thread with a double Command press [1].

bullets.label: Locked computer use:
bullets.text: When enabled, Codex can be triggered from a second device to operate desktop apps even after the Mac is locked and the screen is off [1].

bullets.label: Advanced annotation:
bullets.text: Users can describe changes directly on a web page and instantly preview the results for hands-off site work [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: OpenAI is racing to close the gap with Anthropic while holding its lead over xAI and Google, betting that deeper autonomy - not just more usage - is what wins developers [1]. Goal Mode is a concrete step from assistant to delegate [2].

stories.title: California signs a first-of-its-kind order to shield workers from AI.
stories.toc_summary: Governor Newsom directs state agencies to study severance, worker ownership and faster layoff alerts as AI-driven job cuts mount.
stories.quick_take: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order directing state agencies to study and develop policies protecting workers from AI-driven job losses [1]. It landed a day after Meta laid off 8,000 employees to offset AI investments [1]. With 33 of the world's top 50 AI companies based in California, it is the first state to formally examine what the technology means for workers and the economy [1].

bullets.label: Policy menu:
bullets.text: Agencies will explore severance standards, stock compensation, worker-ownership models and even universal basic capital [1].

bullets.label: Timelines:
bullets.text: Within 90 days the state launches a dashboard tracking AI's job impact; within 180 days agencies pitch WARN Act updates for faster layoff alerts [1].

bullets.label: Labor and revenue:
bullets.text: By Oct. 15 the state will review how unions negotiate AI adoption, update workforce training and explore directing AI revenue toward public benefit [1].

bullets.label: The backdrop:
bullets.text: More than 70,000 tech jobs have already vanished in 2026, with the industry bracing for more cuts as adoption accelerates [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: This is the first concrete sign of a US state treating AI displacement as a policy problem rather than a market outcome [1]. How California defines 'protection' could set the template other states and unions reach for [1].

sources.title: Office of Governor Newsom, via The Rundown AI (email)

stories.title: SpaceX filing reveals Anthropic pays $1.25 billion a month for compute.
stories.toc_summary: An IPO prospectus exposes the staggering scale of Anthropic's compute commitments through 2029.
stories.quick_take: SpaceX's IPO prospectus revealed that Anthropic is paying the company $1.25 billion per month through 2029 for access to compute capacity across Colossus and Colossus II [1]. The disclosure is a rare hard number on the scale of frontier-model compute spend [1]. It underscores how training and serving leading models has become an infrastructure commitment measured in tens of billions of dollars [1].

bullets.label: The number:
bullets.text: Anthropic's payments run at $1.25B per month - roughly $15B a year - through 2029, per the prospectus [1].

bullets.label: Where it goes:
bullets.text: The capacity spans Colossus and Colossus II, the large supercomputing clusters [1].

bullets.label: Diversification:
bullets.text: It fits a pattern of Anthropic spreading compute across providers, alongside reported chip deals with Google (TPUs), Amazon (Trainium) and now Microsoft [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Compute, not headcount, is now the dominant cost line for a frontier lab - and these multi-year commitments lock in demand for chips and power years ahead [1].

sources.title: SpaceX prospectus, via The Rundown AI (email)

stories.title: Anthropic is in talks to run on Microsoft's Maia AI chips.
stories.toc_summary: A potential Maia deal would add a fourth silicon supplier to Anthropic's compute mix.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic is reportedly in talks to use Microsoft's Maia purpose-built AI chips [1]. The move would follow similar arrangements with Google for its TPUs and Amazon for its Trainium silicon [1]. It signals Anthropic's strategy of hedging across multiple chip vendors rather than depending on any single supplier [1].

bullets.label: The talks:
bullets.text: Anthropic is reportedly negotiating to deploy Microsoft's in-house Maia accelerators [1].

bullets.label: A pattern:
bullets.text: It would join existing compute relationships with Google TPUs and Amazon Trainium, broadening Anthropic's silicon base [1].

bullets.label: Why hedge:
bullets.text: Spreading across vendors reduces single-supplier risk and bargaining exposure as compute demand explodes [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: If confirmed, Maia adoption would validate Microsoft's custom silicon and deepen the already tangled web of partnerships among the largest AI players [1].

sources.title: The Information, via The Rundown AI (email)

stories.title: Figure co-founder's new venture Hark raises $700M at a $6B valuation.
stories.toc_summary: Brett Adcock's Hark wants to build personal intelligence with its own models, software and hardware.
stories.quick_take: Figure AI co-founder Brett Adcock's new venture Hark raised $700 million at a $6 billion valuation [1]. The company aims to build its own take on 'personal intelligence,' spanning native models, software and hardware [1]. The raise is one of the largest early bets on a vertically integrated consumer-AI stack [1].

bullets.label: The raise:
bullets.text: Hark closed $700M at a $6B valuation [1].

bullets.label: The pitch:
bullets.text: It is building personal intelligence with native models, its own software and bespoke hardware [1].

bullets.label: The founder:
bullets.text: Brett Adcock previously co-founded humanoid-robot company Figure AI, lending the venture instant credibility with investors [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Full-stack consumer AI - owning the model, the app and the device - is an expensive, ambitious bet; whether Hark can ship hardware that justifies a $6B valuation is the open question [1].

stories.title: Manus weighs a $1 billion raise to unwind its Meta takeover.
stories.toc_summary: Beijing's order to reverse Meta's $2B+ acquisition pushes the agentic-AI startup to seek fresh capital.
stories.quick_take: Agentic-AI startup Manus is exploring options, including a roughly $1 billion raise, to comply with China's order to unwind its $2 billion-plus acquisition by Meta, Bloomberg reports [1]. The forced reversal highlights how geopolitics is reshaping cross-border AI M&A [1]. A new raise would let Manus stand alone again after the deal collapses [1].

bullets.label: The order:
bullets.text: China directed Manus to unwind its $2B+ takeover by Meta [1].

bullets.label: The response:
bullets.text: Manus is weighing options including a ~$1B capital raise to fund independence [1].

bullets.label: The signal:
bullets.text: Beijing's intervention shows regulators willing to block US ownership of strategically sensitive Chinese AI firms [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Cross-border AI deals now carry political risk on both sides; even a closed acquisition can be reversed, forcing startups to keep independent financing on the table [1].

stories.title: Microsoft and EY launch a $1 billion enterprise AI partnership.
stories.toc_summary: Microsoft pairs its engineers and AI with EY's 400,000 consultants to push clients past experimentation.
stories.quick_take: Microsoft and EY announced a new $1 billion partnership to accelerate clients' AI projects [1]. Microsoft will pair its engineers and AI tools with EY's 400,000 consultants to help enterprises scale value creation [1]. The deal explicitly targets the gap between AI pilots and enterprise-wide deployment [1].

bullets.label: The deal:
bullets.text: A $1B initiative combining Microsoft's engineering and AI with EY's global consulting force [1].

bullets.label: The scale:
bullets.text: EY brings 400,000 consultants to drive adoption across client organizations [1].

bullets.label: The goal:
bullets.text: Move enterprises 'beyond experimentation' toward enterprise-wide value creation [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Consulting giants are becoming the distribution layer for frontier AI; partnerships like this help decide whose models end up embedded across the Fortune 500 [1].

stories.title: Harvey's Contract Intelligence lets AI agents redline contracts on their own.
stories.toc_summary: AI agents now do first-pass contract review and markup, escalating only what needs real legal judgment.
stories.quick_take: Harvey launched Contract Intelligence, putting AI agents in charge of first-pass review of inbound contracts [1][2]. The agents apply a firm's own playbooks, write the redlines themselves and show in real time how clauses and negotiation positions trend across the organization [1]. Anything requiring genuine legal judgment is escalated; the rest runs through without a lawyer [1].

bullets.label: What it does:
bullets.text: AI agents take apart incoming contracts, apply in-house playbooks and produce redlines automatically [1][2].

bullets.label: Real-time view:
bullets.text: The system surfaces how clauses and negotiating positions are evolving across thousands of contracts [1].

bullets.label: Human escalation:
bullets.text: Matters needing true legal judgment get escalated; standard review, markup and consistency checks run hands-off [1].

bullets.label: The economics:
bullets.text: Work that Big Law billed for years as associate hours now costs little more than API calls [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: The lowest layer of legal work - standard review and consistency across thousands of documents - is becoming push-button, reshaping how firms staff and price routine contract work [1].

sources.title: Harvey, via The Rundown AI tools (email)

stories.title: Google's Gemini for Science aims to surface connections no one human can see.
stories.toc_summary: A new toolkit bundles models and experiments to help researchers link knowledge across disciplines at scale.
stories.quick_take: Google unveiled Gemini for Science, a toolkit bundling models and experiments meant to make research faster and larger in scale [1]. The premise is that more knowledge already exists than any single person could ever connect [1]. The system tries to close that gap by fusing data across fields and proposing links researchers might otherwise miss [1].

bullets.label: The bundle:
bullets.text: Gemini for Science packages models and experiments aimed squarely at accelerating scientific work [1].

bullets.label: The premise:
bullets.text: Human researchers can't hold all relevant knowledge in their heads; the tool aims to bridge disciplines [1].

bullets.label: The payoff:
bullets.text: By merging cross-domain data, it suggests connections that no individual specialist would surface alone [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: If models reliably propose non-obvious, testable hypotheses across fields, AI shifts from speeding existing research to seeding new directions [1].

stories.title: ChatGPT now builds and edits slides directly inside PowerPoint.
stories.toc_summary: OpenAI embeds ChatGPT in Microsoft PowerPoint so users create and revise slides without leaving the deck.
stories.quick_take: OpenAI integrated ChatGPT directly into Microsoft PowerPoint, so slides can be created and revised by instruction without copying text between a browser and the presentation [1]. The assistant now sits inside the document where the work already happens [1]. For anyone building pitch decks, quarterly reports or training materials, it removes the constant switching between chat window and Office [1].

bullets.label: In-app:
bullets.text: Users create and edit slides via prompts inside PowerPoint, with no browser round-trips [1].

bullets.label: Who benefits:
bullets.text: Frequent deck-builders - pitches, quarterly reports, training material - lose the biggest friction point [1].

bullets.label: The direction:
bullets.text: It continues the trend of AI moving out of a separate chat box and into the tools where knowledge work happens [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Embedding the assistant inside Office is how AI becomes ambient - the value shifts from 'open a chatbot' to 'it's already in the document' [1].

stories.title: Google's Pomelli spins up a full brand website in two clicks.
stories.toc_summary: Pomelli extracts a company's 'business DNA,' builds a brand book, and now ships a hosted landing page.
stories.quick_take: Google is expanding its marketing tool Pomelli into an agentic system [1]. It first pulls a company's 'business DNA' from existing files and images, then generates a full brand book with colors, typography and tone [1]. The new step turns that same brand DNA into a finished landing page in two clicks, hosted directly by Google [1].

bullets.label: Step one:
bullets.text: Pomelli assembles a company's business DNA from its existing files and images [1].

bullets.label: Step two:
bullets.text: It generates a complete brand book - colors, typography, tone of voice [1].

bullets.label: New step:
bullets.text: From the same DNA it now produces a ready landing page in two clicks, hosted by Google [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: For small businesses without a design team, the threshold for a professional brand presence drops to a single prompt run - work that once needed an agency and weeks of lead time [1].

stories.title: Claude Code breaks down token spend per skill, agent and plugin.
stories.toc_summary: A new /usage command turns an opaque monthly bill into a per-component cost center.
stories.quick_take: Claude Code added a /usage command that makes token consumption visible [1]. It breaks down which skills, agents, MCP servers and plugins are pulling how many tokens [1]. A lump-sum bill becomes a cost center per component, giving teams a basis to spot and tune expensive automations [1].

bullets.label: The problem:
bullets.text: Teams get a month-end bill but rarely know which part of their setup caused it [1].

bullets.label: The fix:
bullets.text: /usage attributes token draw across skills, agents, MCP servers and plugins [1].

bullets.label: Rollout:
bullets.text: It starts in the terminal, with the desktop app following right after [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you run agentic workflows, run /usage to find which components dominate your token bill before optimizing anything else [1].

stories.title: Anthropic opens its sixth European office, in Milan.
stories.toc_summary: Europe is Anthropic's fastest-growing region, with revenue up ninefold year over year.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic opened an office in Milan, adding to a growing chain of European locations - London, Dublin, Zurich, Paris, Munich and now Milan [1]. Europe is the company's fastest-growing region, where revenue has risen ninefold year over year [1]. The expansion comes as Anthropic's relationship with the US reportedly cools and it systematically builds out its European presence [1].

bullets.label: The footprint:
bullets.text: Milan becomes Anthropic's sixth European office after London, Dublin, Zurich, Paris and Munich [1].

bullets.label: The growth:
bullets.text: European revenue has grown ninefold year over year, the company's fastest-growing region [1].

bullets.label: For DACH:
bullets.text: It means shorter routes, local points of contact and an AI vendor no longer serving Europe only from afar [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: As Anthropic's US ties reportedly cool, a denser European footprint positions it to win regulated enterprise and public-sector work on the continent [1].

stories.title: High-bandwidth memory now eats 63% of an AI chip's cost.
stories.toc_summary: Epoch AI data shows HBM's share of chip cost climbing from about half to 63% in eight quarters.
stories.quick_take: Per Epoch AI, high-bandwidth memory's share of an AI chip's cost has climbed from about half in Q1 2024 to 63% just eight quarters later [1]. Logic, packaging and everything else now split the remainder [1]. The driver is simple and brutal: each new model generation needs more memory bandwidth per training step [1].

bullets.label: The shift:
bullets.text: HBM went from roughly 50% of chip cost in Q1 2024 to 63% eight quarters on [1].

bullets.label: Why:
bullets.text: Every new model generation demands more memory bandwidth per training step [1].

bullets.label: The winners:
bullets.text: HBM makers SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron capture the rising share [1].

bullets.label: The takeaway:
bullets.text: For anyone planning their own AI hardware, the first bottleneck is memory supply, not logic - and that leverage sits in Korea, not Taiwan [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Memory, not compute logic, is becoming the scarce input that sets AI hardware prices - reshaping who holds pricing power in the supply chain [1].

stories.title: Tesla's Optimus shows a markedly smoother, more human gait.
stories.toc_summary: A new clip shows Optimus walking loosely rather than stiffly - the motor-control milestone humanoids keep tripping on.
stories.quick_take: A new clip shows Tesla's humanoid robot Optimus walking with a markedly smoother gait [1]. The motion looks loose and almost human rather than stiff and mechanical [1]. Natural locomotion is precisely the hurdle that humanoid robotics has repeatedly stumbled on [1].

bullets.label: What changed:
bullets.text: Optimus's walk now looks fluid and natural instead of jerky and machine-like [1].

bullets.label: Why it's hard:
bullets.text: Smooth motor control is the recurring wall where humanoid robots have failed [1].

bullets.label: Why it matters for adoption:
bullets.text: A robot that moves in a stilted way stays a foreign body in factory and home; natural motion is a precondition for acceptance [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Gait quality is a leading indicator for whether humanoids can be deployed around people - watch for it to translate into real tasks, not just demos [1].

stories.title: LeRobot unveils an open-source humanoid for just $2,500.
stories.toc_summary: A mostly-3D-printed biped with a fully open stack drops the price of a walking humanoid by orders of magnitude.
stories.quick_take: LeRobot introduced a two-legged robot built mostly from 3D-printed parts, with the entire stack open: hardware, runtime, simulation, training environments and real-world control [1]. Where walking humanoids cost six figures and came from closed labs, this one runs about $2,500 in materials [1]. Anyone can build, repair and train it themselves [1].

bullets.label: The price:
bullets.text: Material cost is around $2,500, versus six-figure closed-lab humanoids [1].

bullets.label: Fully open:
bullets.text: Hardware, runtime, simulation, training environments and control are all open-source [1].

bullets.label: The shift:
bullets.text: It moves robotics from corporate privilege to a hobbyist platform, much as 3D printing once opened up manufacturing [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The next generation of robotics talent may learn on hardware on their own desk rather than on finished demos - a classic precondition for a field to accelerate [1].

stories.title: China's autonomous barber kiosks scan your head in 3D and cut.
stories.toc_summary: Self-service haircut machines compute a cut line and run the blade with millimeter precision - no staff, no tip.
stories.quick_take: Autonomous barber kiosks are appearing in Chinese cities [1]. The machine captures the head in 3D, computes the cut line and guides the blade with millimeter precision [1]. No appointment, no staff and no tip - a session costs only about 60 yen, per the source [1].

bullets.label: How it works:
bullets.text: It scans the head in 3D, calculates the cut line and executes with millimeter precision [1].

bullets.label: The model:
bullets.text: Fully self-service: no booking, no staff, no tipping, at a very low per-session price [1].

bullets.label: The bigger point:
bullets.text: Even hands-on bodywork - long the domain of steady human hands - is being reduced to calculable geometry a machine solves faster than an apprentice [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: When a craft as tactile as haircutting becomes a solved geometry problem, it reframes which supposedly 'safe' manual jobs automation can actually reach [1].

stories.title: Voicely offers GDPR-compliant AI dictation that works in any app.
stories.toc_summary: A featured tool: AI speech recognition that promises up to 5x faster writing, system-wide.
stories.quick_take: KI Bubble spotlighted Voicely, a GDPR-compliant dictation tool with AI-powered speech recognition that runs in any app [1]. Heavy writers are pitched up to fivefold speed gains by letting the spoken word replace typing [1]. It is positioned as a practical pick for those who want to actually accelerate their writing, not just talk about AI [1].

bullets.label: What it is:
bullets.text: AI speech-to-text that works system-wide across any application [1].

bullets.label: The claim:
bullets.text: Up to 5x faster writing by replacing typing with dictation [1].

bullets.label: The angle:
bullets.text: GDPR compliance is the headline differentiator for European users [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you write a lot and care about EU data rules, a GDPR-compliant dictation layer is a low-risk productivity experiment worth a trial at voicely.de [1].

stories.title: A new guide turns any website into an agent-native CLI.
stories.toc_summary: The Rundown walks through Printing Press to generate command-line tools agents can use against hard-to-reach APIs.
stories.quick_take: The Rundown published a guide on building agent-native CLI tools from any website or API using Printing Press [1]. It shows how to download agent-friendly tools for awkward APIs like Google Flights or ESPN, then build your own [1]. The pitch: when an agent struggles with a specific MCP or integration, have it generate its own commands instead [1].

bullets.label: The tool:
bullets.text: Printing Press generates command-line tools that agents can call against sites and APIs [1].

bullets.label: The workflow:
bullets.text: Install the starter kit, point an agent (Codex, Claude Code, Hermes) at it, then have it build read-only commands for a target site [1].

bullets.label: Pro tip:
bullets.text: If an agent can't use a given MCP or integration, tell it to build its own commands - you just need an API key [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: When an integration is missing or clumsy, generating a thin agent-native CLI is often faster than waiting for an official connector [1].

editorial.title: From assistant to delegate.
editorial.intro: Today's feed reads like a single argument made from a dozen angles: the AI you operate by hand is on its way out, and the AI you hand a goal to is arriving.
editorial.body: Pichai's flip-phone line is the thesis statement, but the products make it concrete. OpenAI's Codex Goal Mode now runs for hours or days off a single objective; Harvey's Contract Intelligence lets agents redline contracts and escalate only the hard parts; ChatGPT moves inside PowerPoint and Pomelli ships a hosted brand site in two clicks. The pattern is autonomy plus ambient presence - AI dissolving into the tools and tasks where work already happens. The infrastructure stories show what that costs: Anthropic paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, in talks for Microsoft's Maia chips on top of Google and Amazon silicon, while memory alone now eats 63% of a chip's price. And the human ledger is right there too - Meta's eight thousand layoffs, Bosch's twenty-two thousand, and California becoming the first state to ask what protection even means.
editorial.pull_quote: The tool that waits for your next command is being replaced by the agent that delivers the result.
editorial.outro: The labs are selling delegation; the policymakers are starting to price its fallout. Both halves of that trade showed up in the inbox on the same morning.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: Autonomy is the through-line - goal-driven agents are moving from coding into legal work, science and slideware, and the binding constraints are now compute, memory and labor policy, not raw capability.
